briefing.text: In mCRPC genomics papers such as the SU2C/PCF study (Robinson et al., Cell 2015), 'clinically actionable' is usually defined broadly by pathway: AR (amplification or mutation), PI3K (PTEN loss, PIK3CA/PIK3CB/AKT1), DNA repair (BRCA2, BRCA1, ATM, CDK12, FANCA, mismatch-repair genes), RAF kinase (BRAF/RAF1 mutations or fusions), CDK/RB (CCND1 amplification, CDKN2A/RB1 loss) and Wnt (APC, CTNNB1). ETS fusions were shown as 'potentially actionable'. A narrow list such as OncoKB level 1 gives a much lower fraction. Count patients with at least one alteration in each category, both separately and together, and report how the fraction changes when AR and ETS are included or left out. This comes from domain knowledge and was not checked against the paper.
briefing.reason: The fraction depends mainly on which genes count as actionable. Teams need the study-style definition and should show how sensitive the result is to it before comparing with 89%.

briefing.text: The claim is about patients, so the denominator should be patients profiled for both mutations and CNA. The clinical tables list about 150 samples, but data_mutations.txt, data_cna.txt, data_sv.txt and data_gene_panel_matrix.txt may each cover a different set of samples. Intersect the sample IDs, map them to PATIENT_ID, and if a patient has more than one sample, count the patient as altered when any sample is altered. Count only protein-altering mutations and only deep CNA calls (+2 amplification, -2 deep deletion).
briefing.reason: A wrong denominator, double-counted patients or low-level CNA calls (+/-1) can shift the fraction by several points around the 89% threshold.

briefing.text: Fusions are found only in data_sv.txt (about 145 rows, mostly TMPRSS2-ERG and other ETS fusions), and that file may not cover every sample. Tabulate the Site1/Site2 gene pairs. Count kinase fusions (BRAF, RAF1) as actionable, and report ETS fusions as a separate layer.
briefing.reason: Including or excluding ETS fusions can change the fraction noticeably, so the choice has to be explicit.

briefing.text: The published figure is believed to include pathogenic germline DNA-repair variants (about 8% of mCRPC, e.g. germline BRCA2/ATM), and a somatic MAF can leave these out. Check data_mutations.txt for Mutation_Status = Germline. If there are no germline rows, expect a somatic-only count to come out a few points below the published figure.
briefing.reason: This affects how a small gap between the computed fraction and 89% should be read.

shared_assumptions: Both teams rebuilt the 'clinically actionable' gene list from memory, using the same broad pathway definition (AR, PI3K, DNA repair, RAF, CDK/RB, Wnt, ETS as a sensitivity check). Neither team checked how much the fraction depends on which genes are in each pathway.

Both counted any non-silent mutation in a pathway gene as actionable. Missense variants of unknown significance in large genes (e.g. ATM, BRCA2, APC) were counted the same as truncating or known-oncogenic events.
Both treated a sample with no SV record as having no fusion, as if all 150 samples had been assessed for fusions.
Both treated the 150 samples as 150 independent patients and used the whole cohort as the denominator.
unused_evidence: data_gene_panel_matrix.txt has a structural_variants column. It shows which samples were actually profiled for SVs. Team B noticed that data_sv.txt covers only 105 samples, but neither team used the matrix to correct the fusion denominator.

Neither team used data_log2_cna.txt or data_cna_hg19.seg to check whether AR or PTEN deep calls in low-purity samples are missed or made up. Team B's purity tertile stratification is the only check that comes close.
Neither team used expression data (e.g. AR, or ETS overexpression without a called fusion) to check fusion or amplification calls, although the study deposited it.
Neither team checked the SV_Status and Center columns in data_sv.txt to confirm that every counted fusion is somatic.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named the reconstructed gene list as their weakest point and reported it, but did not resolve it. The definitions they ran give fractions from about 67% to 97%.

The missing germline calls were noted but not quantified. Neither team counted how many patients are actionable only through a DNA-repair gene, i.e. how much germline addition could move the fraction.
Team A did not run the purity/site stratification. Team B ran it, but did not report whether the fraction drops in low-purity samples.
second_readings: 'Clinically actionable' can be read narrowly, as an event with an approved or investigational targeted therapy, or broadly, as any alteration in a druggable pathway. The narrow reading gives a much lower fraction.
'Affected individuals' means per patient. The fraction also depends on whether the denominator is all sequenced patients or only patients assessed on every platform (mutation, CNA and SV).
'89%' can be read as an approximate figure (about 90%) or as a value the data should reproduce within sampling error. The two readings imply different tolerances.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed True moderately to well. Both teams' study-style definitions bracket 89%, and the hypothesis matches the cohort and the type of claim the source study made. The remaining risk is definitional (gene list, VUS missense, SV coverage) and would most likely shift the estimate by only a few points.

findings.question: In integrative clinical sequencing studies of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, how is a 'clinically actionable aberration' usually defined? Which pathways and alteration types are included, and are germline variants and AR alterations counted?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: every research.py call returned HTTP 403, so this comes from domain knowledge. The SU2C/PCF study (Robinson et al., Cell 2015) reported that about 89% of mCRPC cases had a clinically actionable aberration. It defined actionable broadly: an aberration tied to an approved or investigational targeted therapy, or one that could inform prognosis or treatment. The pathways were AR (amplification, mutation, splice variants), PI3K (PTEN loss, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, AKT1), DNA repair (BRCA2, BRCA1, ATM, CDK12, FANCA, mismatch repair), RAF/MEK (BRAF and RAF1 fusions or mutations), CDK/RB (CCND1 amplification, CDKN2A/CDKN2B loss) and Wnt (APC, CTNNB1). Alteration types were mutations, deep deletions or amplifications, and fusions. AR alterations were counted, as were pathogenic germline DNA-repair variants (about 8%). Without AR the fraction is roughly 65%. ETS fusions were discussed but not central to the 89%.

findings.question: In cBioPortal-style study exports, what does the structural_variants column of a gene panel matrix mean, and does a missing SV record for a sample mean no event or not profiled?
findings.answer: NOT WEB-VERIFIED (HTTP 403). In data_gene_panel_matrix.txt each column after SAMPLE_ID names a molecular profile. The cell holds the gene panel ID (or a WXS/WGS identifier) used to profile that sample for that data type, and NA means the sample was not profiled. A sample with a non-NA value in the structural_variants column but no rows in data_sv.txt counts as profiled with no event detected, so it belongs in the fusion denominator. Samples with NA, or missing from both the matrix and the cases_sv case list, were not profiled and should be excluded.
